It once had 104 columns, each about 17 m tall. 15 still stand.
A 16th column lies on the ground exactly where a storm knocked it down in 1852.
Acropolis
The rock above Athens, crowned by the Parthenon and the Erechtheion with its porch of six stone maidens. The Caryatids on the building are copies; the originals are in the museum.
The Parthenon (447–432 BC) has almost no straight lines: the floor bulges gently upward and the columns swell and lean slightly inward.
In 1687 a Venetian shell hit gunpowder the Ottomans had stored inside the Parthenon, and the explosion blew out its middle.
Legend says Athena won the city by giving it an olive tree, beating Poseidon’s saltwater spring. An olive tree still grows beside the Erechtheion.
Anafiotika and Plaka
Athens’ oldest neighbourhood, with Anafiotika’s island-style cottages tucked above it. Anafiotika has lots of steps.
Plaka has been lived in since Neolithic times, and some streets, such as Adrianou and Tripodon, follow ancient routes.
It’s nicknamed the “Neighbourhood of the Gods” because it sits right below the Acropolis.
Anafiotika was built in the 1800s by builders from the tiny island of Anafi, who came to work on King Otto’s palace and built houses like the ones back home.
A dead-straight 6.4 km slot cut through solid rock between mainland Greece and the Peloponnese.
Emperor Nero broke ground with a pickaxe in AD 67, but the canal wasn’t finished until 1893.
The rock walls rise about 90 m, but at water level it’s only about 25 m wide, too narrow for many modern ships.
At each end is a bridge that sinks under the water to let boats pass over it.
Karytaina
A tiny stone village under a Frankish castle on a steep rock above the Alfeios river, about 20 km off the motorway at Megalopoli. The castle is an open ruin up a steep path.
The castle was built in the mid-13th century by the Frankish baron Geoffrey of Briel.
In 1826 Kolokotronis, the hero of the War of Independence, repaired the walls and used the castle as his base against Ibrahim Pasha.
The five-arched medieval bridge with the castle behind it was on the back of the old 5,000-drachma note, so locals call it “the bridge of the 5,000 drachmas”.
Kalamata
Messinia’s seaside capital, famous for its olives, with a Frankish castle, an old town and a big central market. Paralia Verga is on the coast just east of the city.
On 23 March 1821 Kalamata became the first city the Greeks freed in their War of Independence.
It’s the home of the Kalamatianos, the circle dance you’ll see at every Greek wedding.
Nuns at the Kalograion monastery still weave the city’s famous silk scarves.
Kalamata Central Market
The big municipal market. Local farmers sell here on Wednesday and Saturday mornings.
Sapienza island
An uninhabited green island off Methoni with a lighthouse, beaches and old shipwrecks around it. On the way you cross Navarino Bay, sheltered by the long island of Sphacteria.

On 20 October 1827, British, French and Russian fleets destroyed the Ottoman-Egyptian fleet in Navarino Bay. It was the last major sea battle fought entirely with sailing ships, and it helped secure Greek independence.
In 425 BC the Athenians trapped Spartan soldiers on Sphacteria and 292 surrendered. That shocked the Greek world, because Spartans were thought never to give up.
Sapienza is Italian for “wisdom”. The island has a rare forest of full-size strawberry trees.
Out to sea to the southwest is the Calypso Deep, the deepest point in the Mediterranean at more than 5 km down.
A small village on Navarino Bay next to a protected lagoon that’s a haven for migrating birds.
The lagoon is the only place in Europe where the African chameleon lives.
For many migrating birds it’s the last stop before they fly back across the Mediterranean to Africa, so October is good timing.
Locals call the lagoon Divari, from the Latin “vivarium”, a fish farm.
A perfect Ω-shaped bay of dunes and clear water, with Nestor’s Cave and the ruined Old Navarino castle on the cliff above. The castle is officially closed as unsafe.
It’s thought to be Homer’s “sandy Pylos”, where King Nestor welcomed Odysseus’ son Telemachus.
Myth says the baby god Hermes hid cattle he’d stolen from Apollo in Nestor’s Cave, whose ceiling is about 30 m high.
At the north end of the beach is a Bronze Age beehive tomb traditionally linked to Nestor’s son Thrasymedes.
Niokastro
A large Ottoman fortress above Pylos with a hexagonal citadel, sea bastions and small museums.
The Ottomans built it in 1573, right after their defeat at the Battle of Lepanto, to control the bay.
Its church started life as a mosque and still has its prayer niche (mihrab).
From the late 1800s to the mid-1900s the citadel was a prison, with cells built into its arches.
A huge Venetian sea fortress covering a whole headland. You enter over a 14-arch stone bridge, and at the far end the little Bourtzi tower stands on its own islet.
Venice valued Methoni and nearby Koroni so highly that they were called “the eyes of the Republic”.
Look for carved winged lions of St Mark, the symbol of Venice, on the walls.
The stone bridge at the entrance was built by the French expedition that came in 1828 to help free Greece.
Palace of Nestor
The best-preserved Mycenaean palace in Greece, built around 1300 BC, under a modern roof with raised walkways. Closed Tuesdays.
Archaeologist Carl Blegen found it in 1939, and on the very first day he found clay tablets in Linear B, the earliest written Greek.
The tablets survived because the fire that destroyed the palace baked them hard like pottery.
You can see the throne room and a clay bathtub that legend links to Telemachus’ bath in the Odyssey.
Foneas Beach
A small white-pebble cove south of Kardamyli, split in two by a huge rock where the Foneas gorge meets the sea. The small car park fills early.
Foneas means “killer”. Legend says a pirate once lurked here, though nobody knows if it’s true.
The big rock gives shade, and brave swimmers climb it to jump into the deeper water.
There are caves along the shore, and the clear water is good for snorkelling.
Kardamyli

A stone village between the Taygetos mountains and the sea. Up the lane, Old Kardamyli is the fortified tower complex of the Mourtzinos-Troupakis clan, with the church of Agios Spyridon and a small tower museum.
Homer’s Iliad names Kardamyli as one of seven towns Agamemnon offered Achilles to come back to the Trojan War. It still has the same name.
Writer Patrick Leigh Fermor lived just outside the village for decades. At 18 he walked from Holland to Constantinople, and in 1944 he helped kidnap a German general on Crete.
Local tradition says the tombs of the twins Castor and Pollux are on a trail above the old town.
Exochori viewpoint
A quiet hill village about 450 m up on the edge of the Viros gorge, with a small Byzantine chapel of Agios Nikolaos.
Travel writer Bruce Chatwin’s ashes were laid to rest near the chapel of Agios Nikolaos after he died in 1989.
Chatwin spent months nearby in 1985 writing his bestseller “The Songlines”, close to his mentor Patrick Leigh Fermor.
Stoupa
A relaxed village on a bay, with small, sandy Kalogria beach right next door.
In 1917 the writer Nikos Kazantzakis ran a lignite mine above Stoupa with George Zorbas, the real man behind “Zorba the Greek”.
A bust of Kazantzakis stands on the cliff above Kalogria, said to have been his favourite beach.
Freshwater springs bubble up under the sea here, so the water has refreshingly cool patches.
Viros Gorge
A rocky riverbed path from Kardamyli toward the Agia Sofia church. For keen walkers only.
Langada Pass
The mountain road from Kalamata to Sparta, climbing over Taygetos to about 1,300 m through a gorge with overhanging cliffs and rock tunnels.
Taygetos’ highest peak, Profitis Ilias (about 2,400 m), is the tallest mountain in the Peloponnese.
Ancient writers say the Spartans threw criminals into a chasm called Keadas, which local tradition places near the village of Trypi on this road.
The story that Spartans threw weak babies there doesn’t hold up: the bones found in the pit belong to adults, mostly men aged 18 to 35, and none to infants.
Mystras
A ruined Byzantine city spilling down a hillside near Sparta, with frescoed churches, the Palace of the Despots, a working nunnery and a castle on top.
The last Byzantine emperor, Constantine XI, was proclaimed emperor here in 1449, four years before Constantinople fell.
The nuns of the Pantanassa Monastery are the only people who still live on the site.
The philosopher Gemistos Plethon taught here. His lectures in Florence in 1439 helped spark the Renaissance interest in Plato.
Olive and Olive Oil Museum
A modern museum in Sparta’s old power station on the story of the olive, with presses and a soap-making section. Closed Tuesdays.
Its oldest exhibit is a set of fossilised olive leaves from Santorini, 50,000 to 60,000 years old.
It shows replicas of Linear B clay tablets from the 14th century BC, the earliest written mentions of olive oil.
Working models show olive presses driven by water, steam and diesel.
Diros Caves
At Vlychada, small boats glide through flooded passages lined with stalactites and stalagmites.
Stalactites have been found 71 m under water. They only form in air, so the cave must once have been above the sea.
Bones of panthers, hyenas, lions and even hippopotamuses have been found in the Diros caves.
Next door, Alepotrypa (“fox hole”) was a Stone Age village and burial site until an earthquake sealed its entrance around 3200 BC.
Limeni
A tiny turquoise harbour below Areopoli with fish tavernas, overlooked by the restored tower of the Mavromichalis clan. No sandy beach.
Limeni was the family seat of the Mavromichalis clan, whose leader Petrobey started the 1821 revolution.
Legend says Petrobey’s grandfather married a sea nymph he met on a nearby beach, which locals said explained the family’s good looks.
In 1831 two members of the family assassinated Greece’s first head of state, Ioannis Kapodistrias, in Nafplio.
Areopoli
The main town of the Mani: fortress-like stone tower houses and churches around Taxiarchon Square.
On 17 March 1821 Petrobey Mavromichalis raised the flag of revolution in Taxiarchon Square, starting the Greek War of Independence.
The name means “City of Ares”, the god of war. It was called Tsimova until 1912.
The Mani was known for clan towers and blood feuds. As late as 1870 the army needed artillery to stop a vendetta.
Gytheio
The ancient port of Sparta and the gateway to the Mani: a harbour of fish tavernas, with the pine-covered Marathonisi islet joined to the shore by a causeway.
Tradition says Paris and Helen spent their first night together on Marathonisi (ancient Kranai) after fleeing Sparta, the start of the Trojan War.
The Tzanetakis tower on the islet houses a small museum of the Mani, about travellers who visited it in the 15th–19th centuries.
Myth says Heracles and Apollo founded the town, and its Roman theatre is still used now and then.
Dimitrios shipwreck
A rusting cargo ship beached on Valtaki beach, about 5 km north of Gytheio. Free, no facilities. Don’t climb on it.
It was built in Denmark in 1950 as the Klintholm, about 67 m long.
It was left in Gytheio port in 1980–81 after the captain fell ill and money ran out. A storm in November 1981 tore it loose, and it ran aground here that December.
Legends say it smuggled cigarettes and was set on fire to destroy the evidence. None of that is documented.
Ancient Messene
A large, well-preserved ancient city in a green valley below Mount Ithome, with a theatre, marketplace, sanctuary of Asklepios and a restored stadium, all ringed by massive walls.
The Theban general Epaminondas founded it in 369 BC after beating Sparta at Leuctra, freeing the Messenians from centuries of Spartan rule.
Its wall ran about 9 km with 30 towers, and the road north still passes through the ancient Arcadian Gate.
No later town was ever built on top of it, which is why so much of the city survives.
Mavromati
A small village above Ancient Messene, built around an ancient spring that’s still the village fountain.
Mavromati means “black eye”, a traditional Greek name for a spring.
The ancient writer Pausanias says the nymphs Ithome and Neda bathed baby Zeus in this spring, the Klepsydra, after he was hidden from his father. A good one to tell beside a baby.
Water from the spring was carried every day to the temple of Zeus on top of Mount Ithome.
Polylimnio Waterfalls
A shaded gorge near Charavgi with 15 to 17 green pools linked by small waterfalls, along a rocky trail that’s steep in places.
Polylimnio means “many lakes”.
The Kadoula waterfall drops about 25 m.
Each pool has its own name and folk story, such as Kadi, Mavrolimna and Italou (“the Italian’s”).
Kalamata Castle
Ruins of a 13th-century Frankish castle on a hill above the old town. Prince William II of Villehardouin, who built Mystras castle, was born and died here.
Kalamata Railway Park
An open-air railway museum in the old station, with steam locomotives, carriages and a café. Free.
Archaeological Museum of Messenia
A compact museum in Kalamata’s old market hall, with finds from Mycenaean to Byzantine times.
Nafplio
A Venetian-flavoured harbour town and the first capital of modern Greece, under the Palamidi fortress, with the little Bourtzi castle on an islet in the harbour.
It was Greece’s capital until 1834, when the capital moved to Athens.
The “999 steps” up to Palamidi are a legend: there are about 857 to the entrance. Palamidi costs €20, or €10 reduced.
Kapodistrias, Greece’s first head of state, was shot at the door of Agios Spyridon church in 1831 by two of the Mavromichalis family from Limeni. A bullet mark is still shown under glass.
Free parking, Nafplio
Agamemnon’s legendary citadel, with the Lion Gate, huge “Cyclopean” walls and the beehive tomb called the Treasury of Atreus. Uneven, sloping ground.
A 4th-century BC theatre for about 13,000 people, famous for its acoustics. Guides drop a coin on the stage to show it can be heard from the top rows.

Tzatziki
Cool yogurt dip with cucumber and garlic. Eaten with bread or next to grilled meat.
Strained yogurt, grated cucumber, garlic, olive oil, dill or mint.
Horiatiki (Greek salad)
“Village salad”, the real Greek salad. No lettuce.
Tomato, cucumber, red onion, green pepper, olives, a slab of feta, olive oil, oregano.
Taramosalata
Salty, creamy pink or white dip of fish roe.
Cured fish roe whipped with bread or potato, lemon and olive oil.
Melitzanosalata
Smoky dip of grilled aubergine.
Grilled aubergine, garlic, olive oil, lemon, parsley.
Fava
Silky purée of yellow split peas. Not broad beans, despite the name.
Yellow split peas, onion, olive oil. Topped with raw onion and capers.
Dolmades
Vine leaves rolled around herbed rice, served cool with lemon. The hot version has minced meat and egg-lemon sauce.
Vine leaves, rice, onion, dill, mint, lemon.
Saganaki
A slice of hard cheese fried golden in a small pan, with lemon. “Garides saganaki” is shrimp in tomato and feta instead.
Graviera or kefalograviera cheese, flour, lemon.
Kolokithokeftedes
Fried zucchini fritters, often served with tzatziki.
Grated zucchini, feta, mint, dill, onion, flour.
Horta
Boiled wild or garden greens. Simple, healthy and very Greek.
Seasonal greens (dandelion, amaranth, chard), olive oil, lemon.
Gigantes
Giant white beans baked soft in tomato sauce.
Large white beans, tomato, onion, dill or parsley, olive oil.
Spanakopita
Flaky filo pie with spinach and feta. Tyropita (τυρόπιτα) is the cheese-only version, sold in every bakery.
Filo pastry, spinach, feta, spring onion, dill, egg.
Moussaka
Layers of aubergine, potato and minced meat, topped with thick béchamel and baked.
Aubergine, potato, minced beef or lamb, tomato, cinnamon, béchamel.
Pastitsio
Greek “lasagne”: tube pasta and spiced minced meat under a thick layer of béchamel.
Pasta, minced beef, tomato, cinnamon, béchamel, cheese.
Gemista
Tomatoes and peppers stuffed with herbed rice, baked with potatoes. Some places add minced meat.
Tomatoes, peppers, rice, herbs, olive oil, potatoes.
Stifado
Slow-cooked beef or rabbit stew with lots of small sweet onions.
Beef or rabbit, pearl onions, tomato, red wine, cinnamon, bay leaf.
Kleftiko
Lamb slow-baked in paper or a clay pot until it falls off the bone. The name means “thief-style”.
Lamb, garlic, lemon, oregano, sometimes potatoes and cheese.
